title: AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
authors: Chris Lu, Cong Lu, Robert Tjarko Lange, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, David Ha
abstract: One of the grand challenges of artificial general intelligence is developing agents capable of conducting scientific research and discovering new knowledge. While frontier models have already been used as aids to human scientists, e.g., for brainstorming ideas, writing code, or prediction tasks, they still conduct only a small part of the scientific process. This paper presents the first comprehensive framework for fully automatic scientific discovery, enabling frontier large language models to perform independent research and communicate their findings. We introduce the AI Scientist, which generates novel research ideas, writes code, executes experiments, visualizes results, describes its findings by writing a full scientific paper, and then runs a simulated review process for evaluation. In principle, this process can be repeated to iteratively develop ideas in an open-ended fashion, acting like the human scientific community. We demonstrate its versatility by applying it to three distinct subfields of machine learning: diffusion modeling, transformer-based language modeling, and learning dynamics. Each idea is implemented and developed into a full paper at a cost of less than $15 per paper. To evaluate the generated papers, we design and validate an automated reviewer, which we show achieves near-human performance in evaluating paper scores. The AI Scientist can produce papers that exceed the acceptance threshold at a top machine learning conference as judged by our automated reviewer. This approach signifies the beginning of a new era in scientific discovery in machine learning: bringing the transformative benefits of AI agents to the entire research process of AI itself, and taking us closer to a world where endless affordable creativity and innovation can be unleashed on the world's most challenging problems.

title: Language Models as Compilers: Simulating Pseudocode Execution Improves Algorithmic Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Hyungjoo Chae, Yeonghyeon Kim, Seungone Kim, Kai Tzu-iunn Ong, Beong-woo Kwak, Moohyeon Kim, Seonghwan Kim, Taeyoon Kwon, Jiwan Chung, Youngjae Yu, Dongha Lee, Jinyoung Yeo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in reasoning tasks but still struggle with algorithmic reasoning that requires multi-step logical deduction and precise intermediate results. This paper presents Think-and-Execute, a framework that decomposes the reasoning process of LLMs into two distinct stages: (1) the Think stage, where the LLM generates a step-by-step plan represented as a structured pseudocode program; and (2) the Execute stage, where a deterministic compiler-like module emulates the execution of the pseudocode program to produce the final output. The framework achieves significant improvements in algorithmic reasoning tasks by reducing the reasoning burden on the LLM and ensuring more reliable intermediate computation. Experiments on benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH, and AQuA demonstrate that Think-and-Execute outperforms standard chain-of-thought prompting and other baseline methods.

title: Scientific Hypothesis Generation: Progress and Open Problems
authors: James Evans, Andrey Rzhetsky, Ramesh Raskar, Zachary Horvitz, Daniele Panozzo
abstract: Scientific hypothesis generation is a fundamental step in the research process, requiring creativity, domain knowledge, and the ability to synthesize insights from diverse sources. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models and knowledge graphs, have led to renewed interest in computational hypothesis generation. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of approaches to automated hypothesis generation, categorizing them into literature-based discovery, knowledge graph reasoning, causal inference, and large language model-based methods. We identify key challenges including hypothesis novelty assessment, experimental validation, domain-specific constraints, and integration with laboratory workflows. We also discuss emerging directions such as active learning for hypothesis refinement, uncertainty quantification in generated hypotheses, and human-AI collaborative hypothesis generation. This survey aims to provide a roadmap for researchers interested in developing AI systems that can meaningfully contribute to the scientific discovery process.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Yunfan Gao, Yun Xiong, Xinyu Gao, Kangxiang Jia, Jinliu Pan, Yuxi Bi, Yi Dai, Jiawei Sun, Haofen Wang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities but face challenges such as hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent, untraceable reasoning processes. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating knowledge from external databases. This enhances the accuracy and credibility of the generation, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks, and allows for continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information. In this paper, we comprehensively review existing efforts in RAG in the era of foundation models. We categorize RAG into three paradigms: Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG, and provide a detailed discussion of each paradigm. We also discuss the core components of RAG and describe mainstream evaluation methods. Finally, we highlight current challenges and future research directions, including multi-modal RAG, agent-based RAG, and production-ready RAG systems.

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Hallucination Mitigation Techniques in Large Language Models
authors: S. M. Towhidul Islam Tonmoy, S M Mehedi Zaman, Vinija Jain, Aman Chadha
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in their ability to write human-like text, a key challenge remains: their tendency to hallucinate — generating information that appears to be factual but is not supported by evidence. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of over thirty-two techniques developed to mitigate hallucination in LLMs. We categorize these methods into data-related approaches (pretraining data curation, knowledge augmentation), training-related approaches (RLHF, DPO, supervised fine-tuning with factual data), and inference-time approaches (retrieval augmentation, self-consistency, confidence estimation, post-hoc correction). We also introduce a novel taxonomy of hallucination types that distinguishes between intrinsic hallucination (contradicting the input) and extrinsic hallucination (fabricating facts). We evaluate the strengths and limitations of each approach, discuss trade-offs between factuality and creativity, and identify promising directions for future research including uncertainty quantification and real-time fact verification.

title: Medical Image Analysis with Vision Transformers: A Systematic Review
authors: Jun Ma, Bo Wang, Yuting He, Kun Huang, Xin Wang, Shen Zhao, Jianrong Wu, Xiaoping Yang
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have recently emerged as a powerful alternative to convolutional neural networks in medical image analysis. This systematic review examines the application of ViTs across major medical imaging modalities including radiology, pathology, dermatology, and ophthalmology. We analyze over 200 papers published between 2020 and 2024, categorizing them by task type (classification, segmentation, detection, reconstruction), anatomical region, and imaging modality. Our analysis reveals that ViTs achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks, with particular advantages in capturing long-range dependencies and global context in high-resolution medical images. We identify key challenges including the need for large-scale pretraining data, high computational requirements, and model interpretability in clinical settings. We also discuss hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures that combine the local feature extraction strengths of CNNs with the global reasoning capabilities of Transformers. This review provides practical guidelines for researchers and clinicians implementing ViT-based methods in medical image analysis.

title: Multimodal Medical AI: Unifying Images, Text, and Genomics for Clinical Decision Support
authors: Richard J. Chen, Ming Y. Lu, Drew F. K. Williamson, Tiffany Y. Chen, Jana Lipkova, Zahra Noor, Muhammad Shaban, Maha Shady, Mane Williams, Bumju Joo, Faisal Mahmood
abstract: The practice of medicine is inherently multimodal, requiring clinicians to synthesize diverse data including medical images, textual clinical notes, laboratory values, genomic profiles, and patient histories. Recent advances in multimodal AI have enabled models that can jointly process these heterogeneous data types for enhanced clinical decision support. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for multimodal medical AI that unifies visual, textual, and genomic data through contrastive pretraining and cross-modal attention mechanisms. We evaluate our approach on a diverse set of clinical tasks including differential diagnosis generation, treatment recommendation, survival prediction, and clinical trial matching. Our model, MedFusion, demonstrates that multimodal integration consistently outperforms unimodal and bimodal baselines across all tasks, with particularly significant improvements in rare disease diagnosis and personalized treatment planning. We also address critical challenges in medical multimodal learning: missing modality handling, cross-institution data heterogeneity, and model interpretability. We release a large-scale multimodal clinical dataset spanning five medical centers and three disease areas to facilitate further research.

title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
authors: Alexey Dosovitskiy, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, Matthias Minderer, Georg Heigold, Sylvain Gelly, Jakob Uszkoreit, Neil Houlsby
abstract: While the Transformer architecture has become the de facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. This paper marks the foundational work that demonstrated transformers can be successfully applied to computer vision problems without inductive biases from convolutional architectures.

title: Few-Shot Learning for Medical Image Classification: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
authors: Sheheryar Khan, Hongwei Li, Xinpeng Zhao, Yulun Zhang, Yiwen Zhang, Tariq Mahmood, Rana Faisal Munir
abstract: Medical image classification is fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of expert-labeled data, high inter-class visual similarity, and substantial domain shift across imaging protocols and institutions. Few-shot learning (FSL) provides a promising direction by enabling models to recognize novel disease categories from only a few labeled examples. This survey presents a comprehensive review of FSL methods applied to medical image classification, covering metric learning, meta-learning, data augmentation, and transfer learning approaches. We examine applications across diverse medical imaging domains including X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and histopathology. We identify key challenges unique to medical FSL: anatomical variation, imbalanced disease distribution, domain shift between hospitals and scanners, and the need for clinically interpretable predictions. We also discuss emerging opportunities including self-supervised pretraining for medical images, synthetic data generation using diffusion models, and the integration of radiology reports as auxiliary supervision. Our analysis reveals that while FSL methods show promise, current approaches often fail to generalize to real-world clinical scenarios where disease presentation is highly variable. We provide recommendations for evaluation protocols and benchmarks that better reflect clinical deployment requirements.
